document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Second Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC in response to the Answer filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities 
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
     v. 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
 
 
)  
 
 
)  
) 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. EL25-49-000 
 
 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 
 
 
 
 
Docket No. EL25-20-000 
(Consolidated) 
MOTION FOR LEAVE AND SECOND ANSWER OF 
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC  
Constellation1 moves for leave and submits this second answer in response to the answer 
filed by PJM.2 Constellation sought clarification that generators serving non-firm electricity to 
Co-Located Loads, and that could be recalled during emergencies by both PJM and the 
generator, do not have to delist and needlessly reduce the capacity available for existing PJM 
customers.3 PJM now opposes our request. We reiterate three discrete points in response. 
I. 
Allowing Capacity Resources Serving Non-Firm, Recallable Co-Located Loads to 
Remain Available to PJM is Good Policy 
The Commission should encourage capacity resources serving non-firm, recallable Co-
Located Loads to remain committed to PJM to help meet the system’s resource adequacy needs. 
 
1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) submits this answer and motion for leave pursuant to 
Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213. 
Constellation respectfully submits there is good cause for the Commission to accept this answer as it is intended to 
aid the Commission in its decision-making. 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al. (Mar. 9, 
2026) (“PJM Answer”). 
3 Request for Clarification, or in the Alternative, Rehearing, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al. (Jan. 20, 2026) 
(“Clarification Request”).

2 
This is good and sound policy. Indeed, there are several advantages of encouraging such 
arrangements that align with the Commission’s4 and the Trump Administration’s priorities. 
First, it enhances reliability. Capacity resources serving non-firm Co-Located Loads will 
in fact be available to PJM to help meet resource adequacy needs. As the Commission found, 
large loads are “willing and able to limit [their] energy withdrawals from the transmission 
system.”5 Constellation specifically noted several available mechanisms to ensure Co-Located 
Loads are in fact interrupted when PJM calls upon the generator.6 Forcing the Co-Located 
Generating Facility to relinquish its capacity status needlessly takes megawatts out of the system 
without impacting reliability. 
Second, it saves consumers money. If capacity is lost due to a delist, PJM will need to 
procure additional capacity resources to make up for that loss. It is also possible that, if forced to 
delist, the capacity resource may choose not to serve the Co-Located Load. In that case, PJM 
would also have to procure additional capacity resources and complete more transmission 
upgrades to serve the Co-Located Load.7 These otherwise avoidable costs would be shared 
 
4 See, e.g., Written Testimony of Chairman Laura V. Swett Before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on 
Energy and Commerce, at 2 (Feb. 3, 2026), https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/testimony-laura-v-swett-
chairman-federal-energy-regulatory-commission-us-house (“And in December, we directed the nation’s largest 
grid operator to establish transparent rules to serve AI-data centers and other large loads co-located with 
generation. These rules will safeguard reliability and protect consumers across the mid-Atlantic, impacting over 
67 million Americans.”). 
5 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 159 (2025) (“December 18th Order”); see also id. P 160 
(“Co-Located Load are willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission system under 
certain conditions.”). 
6 See Clarification Request at 5 (“To the extent there are concerns that PJM would be ‘in competition with non-
capacity backed co-located loads for output of a Capacity Resource,’ the Commission could require the Co-
Located Load to disclose information regarding protective relay scheme and its interruptible commitment, and 
impose penalties on that Co-Located Load for failure to comply with its commitment. Those assurances could be 
provided by the Co-located Load confirming its willingness and the ability to interrupt or demonstrating that it has 
back-up diesels or batteries that will take over its supply.”) (footnotes omitted). 
7 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 177 (“[R]equiring such Eligible Customers to take NITS on behalf 
of these Co-Located Loads may in some circumstances result in costly and inefficient transmission system

3 
among all customers. The Commission can save customers these costs by allowing capacity 
resources serving non-firm Co-Located Loads to remain available to help meet the system’s 
resource adequacy needs.  
Third, more large loads would be able to connect faster because more generation would 
be available to serve their needs instead of sitting “idle” round-the-clock as under-utilized 
capacity resources. That advances the Trump Administration’s policy priority of winning the AI 
race by bringing data centers online as soon as possible, while mitigating customer impacts. By 
contrast, forcing generators to delist when they are co-located with data centers receiving non-
firm service runs counter to that policy priority by forcing data centers to choose either NITS 
service, with all the attendant delays and costs associated with transmission upgrades, or pull the 
co-located generator out of the capacity market, even though in choosing non-firm service, the 
data center has made the decision not to be capacity-backed.  
Fourth, it respects the purpose served by the energy market must-offer obligation, 
consistent with the definition of the Capacity Product. Capacity resources serving non-firm Co-
Located Loads are productively serving load that would otherwise have to be served by PJM and 
are recallable to serve PJM grid load when needed.  
II. 
PJM’s Arguments Distinguishing Non-Firm Exports from Co-Located Loads are 
Irrelevant  
PJM’s attempt to distinguish exports from Co-Located Load arrangements misses the 
point. Whether exports are serving other Regional Transmission Organizations that have “their 
 
buildout that may not be necessary if such Eligible Customers are willing and able to take a transmission service 
that requires fewer Network Upgrades to provide, and therefore may result in lower Network Upgrade costs, than 
would NITS.”).

4 
own capacity requirements and resources,”8 or are doing so for potentially only a “limited 
duration,”9 is irrelevant. The key point is that, just like a non-firm export, the energy output of a 
PJM capacity resource serving a non-firm Co-Located Load is not being used to serve PJM 
Network Load and remains recallable by PJM to help the grid meet its resource adequacy needs 
at key times of grid stress. Non-firm exports are not required to delist.10 Neither should capacity 
resources serving non-firm Co-Located Loads. 
III. 
The Commission Has Broad Authority to Require Changes 
We acknowledge that adjustments to PJM’s energy offer price rules may be needed to 
accommodate the non-firm supply of Co-Located Load from a capacity resource.11 Such 
adjustments are not “out of scope” as PJM claims.12 Adjustments to the energy offer rules are a 
logical outcome of Constellation’s timely request for clarification that generators serving non-
firm, recallable Co-Located Load need not delist.13 If the Commission grants clarification or 
rehearing, adjustments may need to be made to implement Constellation’s recommendation to 
allow capacity resources to remain available to help meet the region’s resource adequacy 
needs.14 Making those adjustments is well within the Commission’s powers granted by the 
 
8 PJM Answer at 3. 
9 Id. at 7. 
10 Firm exports are required to delist. See PJM Manual 18, § 4.6.3. (“If a portion of a generation resource is to be 
exported, appropriate documentation must be submitted to PJM to demonstrate that the party exporting the 
generation resource has a financially and physically firm commitment to an external sale of its capacity and 
therefore, is exempt from the offer requirement for capacity resources in Attachment DD, Section 6.6 of the PJM 
Open Access Tariff.”) (emphasis added). 
11 See Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et 
al. at 4 (Feb. 20, 2026). 
12 PJM Answer at 2. 
13 See Clarification Request at 1-6.

5 
Federal Power Act to “modify” its order “in such a manner as it shall deem proper”15 and to 
fashion remedies.16 PJM can propose any necessary revisions in a compliance filing. 
In short, PJM needs to stop finding ways to frustrate the Commission’s efforts to foster 
innovative Co-Located Load arrangements that facilitate new large load while protecting 
customers, and start looking for solutions. “Saying no to innovation is not a winning strategy.”17 
Just as with non-firm exports, PJM could develop rules to accommodate service to non-firm Co-
Located Loads. There are several options that the Commission and PJM may consider exploring, 
including an adjustment to energy market offer levels—either by quantity or price—to reflect the 
delivery of energy to the Co-Located Load as unavailable.  
The Commission and PJM could also consider exempting capacity resources serving non-
firm Co-Located Load from the energy market must-offer rule. There is precedent for this 
approach. The Commission recently approved PJM’s proposal to treat Reliability Must Run 
(“RMR”) units as capacity for Reliability Pricing Model procurement purposes,18 but not impose 
the full suite of Capacity Performance obligations upon them. Specifically, the Commission 
 
14 In fact, additional tariff changes must be made even under PJM’s preferred approach to require delisting. As 
Constellation explained in its Clarification Request, a Capacity Resource can currently only delist under certain 
enumerated circumstances, and serving non-firm Co-Located Load does not fall within those existing exceptions. 
See Clarification Request at 4. 
15 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a). 
16 See, e.g., Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. Fed. Power Com., 379 F.2d 153 (D.C. Cir. 1967) (“[T]he breadth of 
agency discretion is, if anything, at [its] zenith when the action assailed relates primarily not to the issue of 
ascertaining whether conduct violates the statute, or regulations, but rather to the fashioning of policies, remedies 
and sanctions”); FPC v. La. Power & Light Co., 406 U.S. 621, 642, 92 S. Ct. 1827, 32 L. Ed. 2d 369 (1972) 
(finding that the Commission has broad authority to make “pragmatic adjustments” based on circumstances). 
17 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (Rosner, Comm’r, concurring at P 1). 
18 See H.A. Wagner, Joint Offer of Settlement, Docket No. ER24-1787-001, Transmittal Sheet, at 6 (Jan. 27, 2025) 
(“A commitment by Wagner to have its units offered into or administratively cleared in the PJM capacity markets, 
but forbearance by Wagner of any financial remuneration if the units clear and a crediting of those capacity market 
revenues against the CORS costs that are being borne by ratepayers, with any excess capacity market revenues 
being returned to ratepayers.”) (citing Stipulation and Agreement § 4.8; Settled CORS § 5.1(b)).

6 
endorsed an exemption from the energy market must-offer obligation, while nonetheless treating 
the RMR resources as capacity to avoid “PJM over-procuring capacity”19—which in this case 
would occur if the capacity resource serving non-firm load were required to delist. The 
Commission found that these RMR units served a “unique function in PJM” as they would avoid 
“PJM over-procuring capacity,” would be a “reasonable substitute for a capacity resource,” and 
would be “reasonably expected to be available for dispatch by PJM in expectation of any PJM 
emergencies and to perform to address emergencies.”20 Based on this function, the Commission 
found “it reasonable for PJM not to extend to qualifying RMR resources all the rights and 
obligations of capacity resources, including those [specifically] related to [energy market] must-
offer requirements and the imposition of capacity performance penalties.”21 
Capacity resources serving non-firm Co-Located Load also warrant an innovative 
solution, such as an exemption from the must-offer requirements. In fact, as compared to RMR 
units, capacity resources serving non-firm Co-Located Load are actual capacity resources that 
provide significant performance certainty and can be called upon to provide reliability support to 
the grid at any time. They are also subject to full testing, performance and penalty requirements 
of any capacity resource (which are far more stringent performance requirements than those 
applicable to the RMR resources), and just as with the RMRs, “excluding [them] from the 
capacity market supply stack would result in PJM over-procuring capacity.”22  
 
19 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,088, at P 48 (2025). 
20 Id. PP 48-49. 
21 Id. P 49. 
22 Id. P 48.

7 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons stated above, Constellation respectfully requests that the Commission 
accept this Answer and grant its Clarification Request. Capacity resources serving non-firm Co-
Located Load should not be required to delist, needlessly deprive PJM of capacity, and further 
compound the region’s resource adequacy challenges. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
    Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
March 24, 2026
